Main article: [Stanford University endowment](/wiki/Stanford_University_endowment "Stanford University endowment")

Stanford's endowment includes real estate and other investments valued at $36.5 billion as of August 2023,[[130]](#cite_note-133) and is one of the four [largest academic endowments](/wiki/List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_the_United_States_by_endowment "List of colleges and universities in the United States by endowment") in the United States.[[131]](#cite_note-134) The endowment consists of $29.9 billion in a merged pool of assets and $6.6 billion of real estate near the main campus. Stanford is the largest landowner in the Silicon Valley[[132]](#cite_note-135) Payouts from the endowment covered approximately 22% of university expenses in the 2023 fiscal year.[[133]](#cite_note-2023FinRep-136)

Since inception, the university has been the beneficiary of large donations. The endowment began in 1885, six years before the opening of the university, when Leland Stanford and his wife Jane conveyed approximately $20 million to the university.[[134]](#cite_note-137) The university's pioneering of technology intellectual property transfer created both direct investments and enabled a unique pipeline of mega-donors[[135]](#cite_note-138) including from alumni-founded companies with [Google](/wiki/Google "Google") ([Sergey Brin](/wiki/Sergey_Brin "Sergey Brin") and [Larry Page](/wiki/Larry_Page "Larry Page")), [Nike](/wiki/Nike,_Inc. "Nike, Inc.") ([Phil Knight](/wiki/Phil_Knight "Phil Knight")),[[136]](#cite_note-139) [Hewlett-Packard](/wiki/Hewlett-Packard "Hewlett-Packard") ([David Packard](/wiki/David_Packard "David Packard") and [Bill Hewlett](/wiki/Bill_Hewlett "Bill Hewlett")),[[137]](#cite_note-140) and [Sun Microsystems](/wiki/Sun_Microsystems "Sun Microsystems") ([Vinod Khosla](/wiki/Vinod_Khosla "Vinod Khosla"))[[138]](#cite_note-141) as examples. On February 14, 2020, Moonbin appeared in a [V Live](/wiki/V_Live "V Live") broadcast with the other Astro members, officially ending his hiatus.[[68]](#cite_note-68) In celebration of their fourth debut anniversary, Astro released a special digital single album titled *[One & Only](/wiki/One_%26_Only_(Astro_song) "One & Only (Astro song)")* on February 23.[[69]](#cite_note-69) A physical edition of the single was released on March 13.[[70]](#cite_note-70)

In May 4, Astro released their seventh extended play *[Gateway](/wiki/Gateway_(EP) "Gateway (EP)")*.[[71]](#cite_note-71) On May 12, the EP's lead single "Knock" earned the group their second win on the [MBC M](/wiki/MBC_M "MBC M") music show *[Show Champion](/wiki/Show_Champion "Show Champion")*.[[72]](#cite_note-72) On June 28, Astro held their first online live streaming concert 2020 Astro Live on WWW, where they performed the song "No, I Don't" for the first time.[[73]](#cite_note-73) On the same day, the single was distributed digitally through various streaming services.[[74]](#cite_note-74)

On August 14, [Fantagio](/wiki/Fantagio "Fantagio") confirmed that members Moonbin and [Yoon San-ha](/wiki/Yoon_San-ha "Yoon San-ha") would form Astro's first sub-unit called [Moonbin & Sanha](/wiki/Moonbin_%26_Sanha "Moonbin & Sanha") and that the recording for the unit's first [extended play](/wiki/Extended_play "Extended play") had already been completed.[[75]](#cite_note-75) Their debut EP *In-Out*, featuring the lead single "Bad Idea", was released on September 14.[[76]](#cite_note-76)[[77]](#cite_note-77) Eight days later, on September 22, the sub-unit received their first music show award from *[The Show](/wiki/The_Show_(South_Korean_TV_program) "The Show (South Korean TV program)")*, making them the fastest K-pop sub-unit to receive their first win on a music show.[[78]](#cite_note-78)

Narcissus (plant) :: Taxonomy :: Subdivision :: chunk_0011
The infrageneric phylogeny of *Narcissus* still remains relatively unsettled,[[24]](#cite_note-Bastida-25) the taxonomy having proved complex and difficult to resolve,[[14]](#cite_note-FE5-15)[[18]](#cite_note-Medrano-19)[[22]](#cite_note-Mathew-23) due to the diversity of the wild species, the ease with which natural [hybridization](/wiki/Hybrid_(biology) "Hybrid (biology)") occurs, and extensive cultivation and breeding accompanied by escape and naturalisation.[[24]](#cite_note-Bastida-25)[[53]](#cite_note-Zonneveld-54) Consequently, the number of accepted species has varied widely.[[53]](#cite_note-Zonneveld-54)

De Candolle, in the first systematic taxonomy of *Narcissus*, arranged the species into named groups, and those names have largely endured for the various subdivisions since and bear his name as their authority.[[38]](#cite_note-Candollea-39)[[39]](#cite_note-Candolleb-40) The situation was confused by the inclusion of many unknown or garden varieties, and it was not until the work of Baker that the wild species were all grouped as sections under one genus, *Narcissus*.[[49]](#cite_note-Baker-50)

A common classification system has been that of Fernandes [[54]](#cite_note-Fernandes68-55)[[55]](#cite_note-Fernandes75-56)[[56]](#cite_note-Fernandes51-57) based on [cytology](/wiki/Cytology "Cytology"), as modified by Blanchard (1990)[[57]](#cite_note-Blanchard-58)[[58]](#cite_note-Levy-59) and [Mathew](/wiki/Brian_Mathew "Brian Mathew") (2002).[[22]](#cite_note-Mathew-23) Another is that of Meyer (1966).[[59]](#cite_note-Meyer-60) Fernandes proposed two [subgenera](/wiki/Subgenera "Subgenera") based on basal chromosome numbers, and then subdivided these into ten [sections](/wiki/Section_(botany) "Section (botany)") as did Blanchard.[[58]](#cite_note-Levy-59)

Other authors (e.g. Webb[[14]](#cite_note-FE5-15)[[48]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWebb1978-49)) prioritised morphology over genetics, abandoning subgenera, although Blanchard's system has been one of the most influential. The ACS is not a full census but an annual sample-based survey conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau. The language statistics are based on responses to a three-part question asked about all members of a target U.S. household who are at least five years old. The first part asks if they "speak a language other than English at home." If so, the head of the household or main respondent is asked to report which language each member speaks in the home, and how well each individual speaks English. It does not ask how well individuals speak any other language of the household. Thus, some respondents might have only limited speaking ability in those languages.[[12]](#cite_note-13) In addition, it is difficult to make historical comparisons of the numbers of speakers because language questions used by the U.S. Census changed numerous times before 1980.[[13]](#cite_note-14)

The ACS does not tabulate the number of people who report the use of [American Sign Language](/wiki/American_Sign_Language "American Sign Language") at home, so such data must come from other sources. While modern estimates indicate that American Sign Language was signed by as many as 500,000 Americans in 1972 (the last official survey of sign language), estimates as recently as 2011 were closer to 100,000. Various cultural factors, such as the passage of the [Americans with Disabilities Act](/wiki/Americans_with_Disabilities_Act "Americans with Disabilities Act"), have resulted in far greater educational opportunities for [hearing-impaired](/wiki/Hearing_loss "Hearing loss") children, which could double or triple the number of current users of American Sign Language.

The Nobel Prize in Physics has been awarded to 229 individuals as of 2025.[[5]](#cite_note-5) The first prize in physics was [awarded in 1901](/wiki/1901_Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "1901 Nobel Prize in Physics") to [Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen](/wiki/Wilhelm_R%C3%B6ntgen "Wilhelm Röntgen"), of Germany, who received 150,782 [SEK](/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona"). [John Bardeen](/wiki/John_Bardeen "John Bardeen") is the only laureate to win the prize twice—in 1956 and 1972.

[William Lawrence Bragg](/wiki/Lawrence_Bragg "Lawrence Bragg") was the youngest Nobel laureate in physics; he won the prize in 1915 at the age of 25. He was also the youngest laureate for any Nobel prize until 2014 (when [Malala Yousafzai](/wiki/Malala_Yousafzai "Malala Yousafzai") won the Nobel Peace Prize at the age of 17).[[6]](#cite_note-6) The oldest Nobel Prize laureate in physics was [Arthur Ashkin](/wiki/Arthur_Ashkin "Arthur Ashkin") who was 96 years old when he was awarded the prize in 2018.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Only five women have won the prize: [Marie Curie](/wiki/Marie_Curie "Marie Curie") (1903), [Maria Goeppert-Mayer](/wiki/Maria_Goeppert-Mayer "Maria Goeppert-Mayer") (1963), [Donna Strickland](/wiki/Donna_Strickland "Donna Strickland") (2018), [Andrea Ghez](/wiki/Andrea_Ghez "Andrea Ghez") (2020), and [Anne L'Huillier](/wiki/Anne_L%27Huillier "Anne L'Huillier") (2023).[[8]](#cite_note-8) Before L'Huillier, each woman only ever received a quarter share of the prize, although Marie Curie did receive an [unshared Nobel prize in chemistry in 1911](/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Chemistry "List of Nobel laureates in Chemistry"). In 2023, L'Huillier received a one-third share.

There have been six years for which the Nobel Prize in Physics was not awarded (1916, 1931, 1934, 1940–1942). There were also nine years for which the Nobel Prize in Physics was delayed for one year:

* The 1914 prize awarded to [Max von Laue](/wiki/Max_von_Laue "Max von Laue") was announced only in November 1915.[[9]](#cite_note-N1914-9)

Main articles: [Cantons of Luxembourg](/wiki/Cantons_of_Luxembourg "Cantons of Luxembourg") and [Communes of Luxembourg](/wiki/Communes_of_Luxembourg "Communes of Luxembourg")

Further information: [Administrative divisions of Luxembourg](/wiki/Administrative_divisions_of_Luxembourg "Administrative divisions of Luxembourg")

Luxembourg is divided into 12 [cantons](/wiki/Cantons_of_Luxembourg "Cantons of Luxembourg"), which are further divided into 100 [communes](/wiki/Communes_of_Luxembourg "Communes of Luxembourg").[[112]](#cite_note-115) Twelve of the communes have [city status](/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Luxembourg "List of cities in Luxembourg"); the city of [Luxembourg](/wiki/Luxembourg_City "Luxembourg City") is the largest.[[113]](#cite_note-116)

Partitions and cantons of Luxembourg

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/LuxembourgPartitionsMap_english.png/330px-LuxembourgPartitionsMap_english.png)](/wiki/File:LuxembourgPartitionsMap_english.png)

There have been three [partitions of Luxembourg](/wiki/Partitions_of_Luxembourg "Partitions of Luxembourg") between 1659 and 1839. Together, they reduced the territory of Luxembourg from 10,700 km2 (4,100 sq mi) to the present-day area of 2,586 km2 (998 sq mi). The remainder forms parts of modern-day Belgium, France, and Germany.

The producers wanted [Courteney Cox](/wiki/Courteney_Cox "Courteney Cox") (*pictured*) to portray Rachel; however, Cox wanted to play Monica and co-creator Marta Kauffman agreed after watching the audition.

Once it became apparent that the series was a favored project at NBC, Littlefield reported that he was getting calls from every agent in town, wanting their client to be a part of the series.[[7]](#cite_note-friendsorigin-7) Auditions for the lead roles took place in New York and Los Angeles.[[46]](#cite_note-friendswrit-46) The casting director shortlisted 1,000 actors who had applied for each role down to 75. Those who received a callback read in front of Crane, Kauffman and Bright. At the end of March, the number of potential actors had been reduced to three or four for each part, and these actors were asked to read for [Les Moonves](/wiki/Leslie_Moonves "Leslie Moonves"), then president of Warner Bros. Television.[[47]](#cite_note-Kolbert2-47)

Having worked with David Schwimmer in the past,[[46]](#cite_note-friendswrit-46) the series creators wrote the character of Ross Geller with him in mind, and he was the first actor cast.[[48]](#cite_note-48) Courteney Cox wanted to play the role of Monica Geller because she liked the "strong" character, but the producers had her in mind to play Rachel Green because of her "cheery, upbeat energy", which was not how they envisioned Monica; after Cox's audition, though, Kauffman agreed with Cox, and she got the role.[[37]](#cite_note-friendsorigins1-37)[[49]](#cite_note-49) When Matt LeBlanc auditioned for Joey Tribbiani, he put a "different spin" on the character.[[37]](#cite_note-friendsorigins1-37) He played Joey more simple-minded than intended and gave the character heart.
